card_summary: Latency and signal integrity are paramount in live signal transport, and the use of protocols like ST 2110 and SRT can significantly impact these factors. In live production environments, maintaining Genlock and ensuring frame-accuracy are crucial for a coherent output. In practice, this means engineering teams must carefully evaluate the trade-off between transport protocol overhead and the resulting latency, particularly when working with high-bandwidth formats like 12G-SDI or JPEG XS. The real challenge is achieving reliable, low-latency signal transport while maintaining signal integrity, which will be critical for live events like the Night Landscapes at Llum BCN 2026.

Why Real-Time Transport Protocols Are Forcing Broadcasters to Rethink Signal Integrity

As live production workflows become increasingly complex, the pressure to maintain signal integrity and minimize latency is mounting. With the rise of IP-based infrastructures, broadcasters are being forced to re-evaluate their approach to real-time transport protocols. The shift towards IP-based workflows has introduced new challenges, including packet loss, jitter, and latency, which can significantly impact the quality of live broadcasts.

What This Development Actually Means

The recent adoption of ST 2110, a suite of standards for professional media over managed IP networks, marks a significant development in the industry. This standard provides a framework for the transport of uncompressed video, audio, and metadata over IP networks, enabling broadcasters to build more flexible and scalable live production workflows. The use of ST 2110, in conjunction with other protocols such as NDI and SRT, is becoming increasingly prevalent in live production environments.

The industry context for this development is the growing demand for high-quality, low-latency live video streaming. As consumers increasingly expect high-definition, low-latency video, broadcasters are under pressure to deliver. The use of real-time transport protocols such as ST 2110, NDI, and SRT is critical to meeting this demand, as they enable the efficient and reliable transport of high-quality video signals over IP networks.

Why It Matters for Broadcast Operations

The adoption of real-time transport protocols such as ST 2110, NDI, and SRT has significant implications for broadcast operations. For example, the use of ST 2110 enables broadcasters to build more flexible and scalable live production workflows, while the use of NDI and SRT provides a more efficient and reliable means of transporting video signals over IP networks. Vendors such as Matrox, with their ConvertIP gateway, and Riedel, with their MediorNet solution, are already supporting these protocols in their products. Meanwhile, companies like Evertz, with their Mediator-X platform, are leveraging these protocols to enable more efficient and scalable live production workflows. As a result, broadcasters will need to carefully evaluate their infrastructure decisions over the next 12-18 months, considering the trade-offs between CapEx and OpEx, integration complexity, and workflow disruption.

Impact by Stakeholder

  • Regional and national broadcasters: Will need to budget for the deployment of ST 2110-compatible equipment, such as IP gateways and switches, to support the transport of uncompressed video and audio over IP networks. This will enable them to reduce transmission costs, lower latency, and simplify signal routing, while also reducing their hardware rack footprint.
